Intro Chemistry I¶

Chapter 1¶

Basic Concepts About Matter¶

Cengage Chapter 1 Link on Canvas

Lecture ppt slides Link

Click Here to watch Solid-Liquid-Gas video demo

  • Chemistry, Matter, Physical States of Matter. What is chemistry? What is matter? Know the three physical states of matter and be able to define the differences between them.
  • Physical versus Chemical changes. Be able to make the distinctions between physical properties versus chemical properties and physical change versus chemical change.
  • Classification of Matter. Know the differences between a pure substance versus a mixture, and an element versus a compound.
  • Understand what is element, atoms, chemical symbol, molecules (homoatomic), compounds (heteroatomic), pure substance, mixture (homogenous/heterogenous), chemical symbol, chemical formula.

Concept Checks and/or Class Practice¶

  • To measure the boiling point of a substance, a liquid must be changed into a gas. Why is boiling point considered a physical property when a gas’ appearance is much different from that of a liquid?

  • The physical states of matter are: (a) solid, liquid, and gas. (b) solid, liquid, and heat. (c) solid, liquid, and electricity. (d) liquid, electricity, and heat.

  • Which one of the following is an example of a chemical change? (a) Pulverizing (crushing) rock salt (b) Burning of wood (c) Dissolving of sugar in water. (d) Melting a popsicle on a warm summer day.

  • Which of the following is a property of both gases and liquids? (a) definite shape (b) indefinite shape (c) definite volume (d) indefinite volume.

  • Which of the following statements concerning the properties of matter is false? (a) Properties of matter are of two types: physical and chemical. (b) A physical property is a characteristic of matter that can be observed without changing its basic identity. (c) A chemical property describes the way matter undergoes or resists change to form a new substance. (d) One example of the physical property of water is that it can be broken down into hydrogen and oxygen gases.

  • When a substance undergoes a chemical change, it is always true that: (a) it melts. (b) it changes state. (c) its chemical composition changes. (d) heat is released. (e) none of the above.

  • How to differentiate among atom, element, compound, molecule with examples?

  • The difference between an element and a compound is: (a) an element is a pure substance, whereas a compound is not. (b) an element can be broken into simpler constituents by physical means, whereas a compound can not. (c) an element can be broken down into a simpler substance by chemical means, whereas a compound can not. (d) an element cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means, whereas a compound can.

  • Which of the following contain only pure substances? (a) Oxygen, tap water, glass of tea (b) Oxygen, glucose (a simple sugar), silver (c) Glucose, chocolate chip cookies, wood (d) Gasoline, dirt, rocks.

  • A substance is composed of diatomic molecules. Choose the appropriate classification from the response list below: (a) could be an element or a compound (b) could be an element but not a compound (c) could be a compound but not an element (d) could not be an element nor a compound.

  • Justify with an explanation what kind of changes, physical or chemical? (a) mixing sugar into water is (b) Nitrogen gas and oxygen gas formed nitric-oxide gas (c) table salt in water.

  • Justify as element/compound/molecule: (a) water (b) oxygen gas.

  • Which of the following is a homogeneous mixture? (a) Pure water (b) Gasoline (c) Jar of jelly beans (d) Soil (e) Copper metal.

  • A pure substance that can be broken down into simpler pure substances by chemical means is called a(n): (a) element (b) compound (c) homoogeneous mixture (d) heterogeneous mixture.

  • Chemical symbols consist of: (a) the first letter of the element’s name always in lower case. (b) one- or two-letters derived from the element’s name with both letters always capitalized. (c) the first two letters of the element’s name with both letters capitalized. (d) one- or two-letters derived from the element’s name with the first letter capitalized and the second in lower case.

  • For each of the following chemical formulas, determine how many atoms of each element are present:

  • Chemical formulas consist of: (a) symbols of each element in a compound with all letters capitalized. (b) symbols of each element in a compound with all letters in lower case. (c) symbols of each element in a compound with numerical subscripts to indicate the number of atoms of each element in the compound. (d) symbols of each element in a compound.

  • An electrical current is applied to 50 mL of water. After a period of time, there is nothing left in the container because: (a) a physical change occurs resulting in the formation of a gas. Since water is a heterogeneous mixture, its components are also changed to gas. (b) a physical change, evaporation, occurs and as there is no residue, water is a pure substance. (c) a chemical change takes place converting water to its elements, hydrogen and oxygen. No residue is left because water is a pure compound. (d) a chemical change takes place, but water is a heterogeneous mixture and its components are converted to gases.

  • You are given two cylinders, each containing a gas. You are requested to test the flammability of each gas, and you discover that one gas is very flammable, but the other gas extinguishes the flame. The two gases are _____ and _____ and are classified as a _____ and _____, respectively. (a) hydrogen; methane; homoatomic molecule; heteroatomic molecule (b) hydrogen; carbon dioxide; diatomic molecule; heteroatomic molecule (c) neon; carbon dioxide; element; diatomic molecule (d) hydrogen; oxygen; element; element

Chapter 2¶

Measurements in Chemistry¶

Cengage Chapter 2 Link on Canvas

Lecture ppt Slides Link

Click Here to watch Density ia an intensive property

  • Measurements, Metric System. Understand the importance of including a unit with a measured or calculated value in science. Be familiar with the metric system of units and prefixes. Know how to convert between the name, the prefix, and the power of ten without any help for these six prefixes: mega (M), kilo (K), deci (d), centi (c), milli (m), micro (μ).
  • Significant Figures. Be able to recognize an exact number. Understand that every measurement has a certain level of uncertainty associated with it. Be able to determine the proper number of significant digits in: (a) a number in decimal notation; (b) a number in scientific notation; or (c) an answer to a series of mathematical calculations.
  • Exponents/Scientific Notation. Know how to interpret scientific notation and be able to interconvert any number between decimal notation and scientific notation.
  • Conversion Factors/Dimensional Analysis. Be able to use conversion factors to convert from one unit to another unit. Know how to use dimensional analysis to help set up and check your calculations. Temperature. Understand the Celsius and Kelvin temperature scales. You should memorize the conversion factor to interconvert between these two scales.
  • Density. Understand how density is calculated. Be able to use density as a conversion factor to interconvert between mass and volume.

Concept Check and/or Class Practice¶

  • What system of measurement is used in scientific work? (a) English system (b) European system (c) Metric system (d) Science system.

  • Which of the following represents the largest measurement of mass of an object? (a) Gram (b) Microgram (c) Nanogram (d) Kilogram.

  • Which of the following statements is true? (a) An exact number is a number that has no uncertainty associated with it. (b) An inexact number is a number that has a degree of uncertainty associated with it. (c) Inexact numbers occur any time a measurement is made. (d) All of these.

  • Which types of zeros in a number are considered significant? (a) Leading and confined zeros (b) Leading and trailing zeros (c) Confined and trailing zeros (d) Leading, confined, and trailing zeros.

  • Read the length of the metal bar with the correct number of significant figures.

(a) 20 cm (b) 15 cm (c) 15.0 cm (d) 15.00 cm (e) 15.000 cm.

  • how many Significant figures in 1006.00, 10060, 0.0060, 1006 ?

  • A calculator gives an answer of 8.8274 when you multiply 4.60 by 1.919. In which of the following is the answer rounded to the correct number of significant figures? (a) 8.83 (b) 8.82 (c) 8.829 (d) 8.8.

  • After a series of calculations, a scientist obtains an answer of 0.045006700 on a calculator. If this answer has four significant figures, how should it be written? a) 0.045 b) 0.0450 c) 0.04500 d) 0.04501 e) 0.045007.

  • Converting 630179 to significant notation with four significant figures gives
    (a) 6.301 x 10^5 (b) 6.302 x 10^5 (c) 6301 x 10^5 (d) 6302 x 10^5.

  • When expressed in scientific notation in a way that preserves the original number of significant figures, the measured numbers 3200 and 3200.0 become, respectively, (a) 3.2 x 10^-3 and 3.2000 × 10^-3 (b) 3.200 × 10^-3 and 3.2000 × 10^-3 (c) 3.2 × 10^3 and 3.2 × 10^3 (d) 3.2 × 10^3 and 3.2000 × 10^3 (e) 3.200 × 10^3 and 3.2000 × 10^3.

  • Which of the following is the correct conversion factor to convert 4.00 inches to 10.2 cm? (a) 1.00 inch/2.54 cm (b) 25.4 mm/1.00 inch (c) 2.54 cm/1.00 inch (d) 25.4 cm/1.00 inch.

  • If an individual took 300 mg of trazodone each evening before bedtime for one year, how many pounds of trazodone would he or she consume? There are 454 g in a pound (a) 2.411894 (b) 2.4 (c) 2.412 (d) 0.241.

  • Perform the following conversion 586.7 μm = _________ km. (a) 5.867×10^-9 b) 5.867×10^-7 c) 5.867×10^-4 d) 0.5867 e) 5.867×10^9.

  • The mass of a sodium sample is 2550 g. What would be the mass in kilograms? (a) 0.255 kg b) 2.55 kg c) 25.5 kg d) 255,000 kg e) 2,550,000 kg.

  • The typical temperature of a laboratory rat is 41°C. What is this temperature in Kelvin? a) -232 K b) -196 K c) 278 K d) 314 K.

  • If you were given a pound of feathers and a pound of lead, the density of each would be _____ because _____. (a) the same; they have the same mass (b) the same; they have the same volume (c) different; the mass of lead is greater than the mass of feathers (d) different; they have different volumes.

  • The density of mercury in 13.5 g/mL. A mass of 50.0 g would occupy how many milliliters of volume? (a) 0.270 mL (b) 3.70 mL (c) 36.5 mL (d) 675 mL.

Chapter 3¶

Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table¶

Cengage Chapter 3 link on Canvas

Lecture ppt slide Link

  • Atomic Structure. Understand how an atom is composed of subatomic particles (protons, neutrons and electrons) and the properties and locations of the sub-atomic particles within the atom. Know how to draw correct complete chemical symbol for an atom containing protons, neutrons.
  • Isotopes. Know what an isotope is. If given an isotopic symbol (F-19) be able to find the correct number of protons, neutrons and electrons (9p+, 10n, 9e-).
  • Periodic Law and Table. What is the periodic law and how is it related to the periodic table? On the periodic table, be able to identify: a) groups and periods; b) an element if given its group and period c) the alkali, alkaline earth, halogen and noble gas groups; d) metals and nonmetals; and e) the representative (main group) elements, transition metal elements and inner transition metal elements.
  • Electronic Structure of Atoms. Understand how electrons in atoms are organized into electron shells, subshells and orbitals and how each of these levels of organization is defined. Be able determine how many subshells exist within a given shell and be familiar with the letter designations for subshells (s, p, d, and f). What do all orbitals of a given subshell have in common? How many electrons can fit in one orbital?
  • Electron Configurations. Understand how electrons are configured within an atom using orbital diagrams. Know the subshell filling order of the periodic table and how many electrons can fit into each subshell type. Be able to generate the correct electron configuration for any element using either an orbital diagram or the shorthand notation (e.g. for C, 1s22s22p2). Understand how electron configurations explain the periodic law.

Concept Check and/or Class Practice¶

  • The subatomic particles of an atom are: (a) protons and neutrons. (b) protons and electrons. (c) neutrons and electrons. (d) protons, neutrons, and electrons.

  • What is the correct complete chemical symbol for an atom containing 25 protons and 30 neutrons?

  • The atomic number of an atom is: (a) the sum of the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. (b) the number of neutrons in the nucleus of an atom. (c) obtained from the mass number. (d) the number of protons and the number of electrons in an atom.

  • Atoms of an element that contain a different number of neutrons are known as: (a) nucleophiles. (b) isotopes. (c) isophiles. (d) neutrophiles.

  • which of the following element is isotopes?

  • Elements are arranged in the periodic table according to: (a) increasing number of neutrons. (b) increasing number of neutrons and protons. (c) increasing atomic number. (d) increasing atomic mass unit.

  • An atom contains 33 protons, 35 neutrons and 33 electrons. The atomic number and mass number for this atom are, respectively, (a) 35 and 33 (b) 33 and 35 (c) 33 and 66 (d) 33 and 68 (e) 35 and 68

  • Differences between metals and nonmetals are: (a) metals conduct electricity while nonmetals do not. (b) metals are generally solids while nonmetals exist as gases, liquid, or solids. (c) metals are malleable while nonmetals are brittle in the solid state. (d) all of these.

  • The space in which electrons move rapidly about a nucleus is divided into: (a) shells and subshells. (b) shells, subshells, and orbitals. (c) shells and orbitals. (d) subshells and orbitals.

  • The electron configuration of sodium is
    (a) 1s21s22p63s1 (b) 1s22s22p63s1 (c) 1s22s22p7 (d) 1s22s12p63s1

  • Elements within vertical columns in the periodic table share similar chemistry. These columns are called: (a) shells (b) subshells (c) orbitals (d) periods (e) groups

  • Columns in the periodic table are known as groups. Elements in groups have similar chemical properties because they contain the same number of: (a) total electrons. (b) protons. (c) outer shell valence electrons. (d) neutrons.

  • Consider two elements: One is a gas and the other is a solid. Each contain identical number of electrons in their outer shell. These elements are _____ and _____. They contain _____ and _____ neutrons, respectively. (a) F; I; 10; 74 (b) N; S; 14; 32 (c) O; S; 16; 32 (d) F; I; 19; 127

  • You are asked to determine the composition of a gas. There are three components with three different applications. They all have the same atomic number, but the number of neutrons is zero, one, and two, respectively. One of the components is used as a radioactive tracer in biological experimentation. Identify the gas you were given. How are the three components referred? What are the names of each component? (a) Carbon; isotopes; carbon-12; carbon-13; and carbon-14 (b) Hydrogen; isotopes; protium; deuterium; and tritium (c) Hydrogen; elements; protium; deuterium; and tritium (d) Oxygen; elements; oxygen-8; oxygen-15; and oxygen-16

  • How many electrons and protons are in Na+ ion (cation) contain, Na is which group element in the periodic table and how many valence electrons(s) are in Na?

Chapter 4¶

Chemical Bonding: The Ionic Bond Model¶

Cengage Chapter 4 Link on Canvas

Lecture ppt slides link

  • Chemical bonding. What is a chemical bond? Understand the difference between an ionic bond (electron transfer) and a covalent bond (shared electrons)
  • Ionic versus covalent compounds. What simple experimental test can be used to determine if a compound is ionic or covalent (i.e. lecture demonstration)? Be able to determine if a compound is ionic or covalent from its molecular structure.
  • Ions. Understand how atoms can gain or lose electrons to form anions (negatively charged ions) or cations (positively charged ions). Be able to quickly interconvert between the number of protons and electrons in an ion and the ionic symbol (e.g., O2 8P, 10E).
  • Molecular Compound Lewis Structures. Be able to draw the Lewis structure of a molecular compound. Understand how many bonds each element typically forms and how to form double and triple bonds.
  • Octet Rule, periodic trends in ion charges and valence electrons. Understand what the octet rule is. Know which elements tend to form cations, which elements tend to form anions, and the periodic patterns for the charges of the cations and anions of representative elements. (Lecture)
  • Ionic Compound Formula Unit. Understand that ionic compounds exist in an extended array of alternating cations and anions and no separate “molecules” of ionic compounds exist. What does the formula unit of an ionic compound represent?
  • Simple Ionic Compound Naming. Be able to interconvert between formula name for simple binary ionic compounds. Understand how to name binary ionic compounds containing cations with a fixed charge and cations with a variable ionic charge.
  • Physical properties of ionic compounds. Understand melting points, boiling points and aqueous solution of ionic compounds. (Lecture)
  • Polyatomic Ion Compound Naming. Know how to name polyatomic ions and compounds containing poly atomic ions. Memorize the formulas/charges/names of the polyatomic ions: nitrate, nitrite, ammonium, sulfate, hydrogen sulfate, sulfite, hydrogen sulfite, phosphate, hydrogen phosphate, dihydrogen phosphate, phosphate, carbonate, hydrogen carbonate, acetate, hydronium, and hydroxide.

(d) Lewis symbols or electron-dot symbols.

Chapter 05¶

Chemical Bonding: The Covalent Bond Model¶

Cengage Chapter 5 Link on Canvas

Lecture ppt slides link

  • Covalent Bond. Understand what a covalent bond is and how it differs from an ionic bond. Know how to use both the electron dot and dash notations to represent a covalent bond.
  • Molecular Compound Lewis Structures. Be able to draw the Lewis structure of a molecular compound. Understand how many bonds each element typically forms and how to form double and triple bonds.
  • Systematic Process for Drawing Lewis Structures. Using the systematic process described in the text and lecture to draw the Lewis structure of any molecular compound. Understand the principles presented in lecture in which electonegativity and bond polarity can be used to determine the correct “skeleton” structure.
  • Electronegativity and Bond Polarity. Understand what electronegativity is and the periodic trends in electronegativity in the representative elements of the periodic table. Understand how to represent the unsymmetrical distribution of electrons in a polar bond. Be able to sort a series of bonds in order of increasing polarity.
  • Molecular Geometry. Understand the VSEPR principles used to predict molecular geometry. Be able to VSEPR principles to predict the electron group arrangement and molecular geometry of a molecular compound. (Lecture)
  • Molecular Polarity. Based upon the presence of polar bonds and the molecular geometry, be able to determine if a molecule is polar (unsymmetrical distribution of e- charge) or nonpolar (symmetrical distribution of e- charge).

Concept Check and/or Class Practice¶

  • A covalent bond occurs when: (a) there is a transfer of electrons only between similar or identical atoms. (b) there is a transfer of electrons only between similar atoms. (c) there is a sharing of valence electrons between similar or identical atoms. (d) there is a sharing of electrons between a metal and nonmetal.

  • What is the difference between bonding electrons and lone electron pairs? (a) Bonding electrons are valence electrons that are shared between atoms and lone electron pairs are nonbonding electrons. (b) Bonding electrons are shared between two identical atoms and lone electron pairs are shared between two nonidentical atoms. (c) Bonding electrons and lone electron pairs are interchangeable terms used to identify electrons in a covalent bond. (d) Bonding electrons are involved in the formation of covalent bonds and lone electron pairs are involved in formation of ionic bonds.

  • How many electrons are shared in a double covalent bond? (a) 2 (b) 4 (c) 6 (d) 8

  • How many covalent bonds can oxygen form? (a) 1 (b) 2 (c) 4 (d) 8

  • Draw a Lewis structure for each of the following molecules (a) H2 (b) F2 (c) HF (d) NH3 (e) CO2 (f) CCl4

  • Determine the shape for each of the following molecules, and mention their bond angles (a) HCN (b) NH3
    (c) O3

  • Which of the following elements has the highest electronegativity? (a) H (b) He (c) O (d) Cl

  • Arrange the following bonds in the descending order of polarity (a) N–F O–F C–F (b) C–F N–O Si–F (c) Cl–Cl B–Cl S–Cl

  • Which of the following bonds would be the least polar/most polar yet still be considered polar covalent/without being considered ionic? (a) Mg–O (b) C–O (c) O–O (d) Si–O (e) N–O

  • Which statement best describes a polar covalent bond? (a) In a polar covalent bond, there is equal sharing of electrons between two atoms. (b) In a polar covalent bond, there is unequal sharing of electrons between two atoms. (c) In a polar covalent bond, there is equal sharing of electrons between identical atoms. (d)In a polar covalent bond, there is unequal sharing of electrons between identical atoms.

  • Which of the following molecules are polar? (a) F2 (b) HF (c) NH3 (d) SO2 (e) CCl4 (f) CO2 (g) BeCl2 (h) H2O (i) CH4

  • Which of the following compounds is named incorrectly? (a) NO2 nitrogen dioxide (b) P2O5 phosphorus pentoxide (c) PCl3 phosphorus trichloride (d) SO3 sulfur trioxide (e) ICl iodine monochloride

  • A liquid molecular compound is given to you and you are told to handle it with caution. It can cause damage or death if it is consumed in large quantities, if it enters your lungs, if you are hit with a frozen chunk of this material, or if a hot solution of it is spilled on you; however, this liquid is necessary to sustain life. The liquid is a pure molecular compound, has no taste, and is known to contain hydrogen and oxygen. Identify the liquid, its molecular geometry, and whether it is polar or nonpolar. (a) Water; linear; polar (b) Water; linear; nonpolar (c) Water; angular; nonpolar (d) Water; angular; polar

Chapter 06¶

Chemical Calculations: Formula Masses, Moles, and Chemical Equations¶

Cengage Chapter 6 Link on Canvas

  • Mole Concept and Calculations. Understand what chemists mean by the term mole. Be able to use the mole concept in the following calculations:

converting between numbers of particles and moles, converting between mass and moles, and converting between moles of a compound and moles of atoms in the compound. Be able to combine all three of these types of calculations together in a series to do any calculation.
